sections.heading: Wanting you more than anything else
sections.text:
My dear Lord, you already know what is in me, but I want to say it plainly: I want you. More than comfort, more than success, more than a good feeling about my life, I want to belong to you completely. I want holiness. I want my will brought into line with yours.

You are the one who put these desires in me, and you are the only one who can satisfy them. So I bring them back to you. Make this longing real, steady, and deeper than anything else I chase.
theological_themes: Desire for God above all created goods
Holiness as conformity to God's will
God as the giver and fulfiller of holy desires

scripture_references.connection: The psalm gives language to a soul that is not merely seeking relief but seeking God himself. It supports the prayer’s central longing for communion with God as the deepest desire of the heart.
Paul teaches that God works in his people both to will and to work for his good pleasure. This grounds the confession that holy desires come from God and must be fulfilled by God’s own power.

sections.heading: Asking to be changed from the inside
sections.text:
I want real fellowship with you, not just thoughts about you. I want the sin still living in me to be put to death, especially the pride that can hide inside spiritual things. Keep me from admiring my own growth, my own prayers, or my own experiences.

Give me a clear, tender understanding of what true godliness is. Show me the beauty of holiness—not as a religious performance, but as a life shaped by Christ.
theological_themes: Communion with God
Mortification of remaining sin
Spiritual pride as a subtle corruption
True godliness centered on Christ and expressed in holiness

scripture_references.connection: This passage connects life in the Spirit with putting to death the deeds of the body. It supports the prayer’s request for real inward change rather than surface religion.
James warns that God opposes the proud and gives grace to the humble. This speaks directly to the prayer’s concern over spiritual pride, especially pride disguised as devotion.
Paul describes the mystery of godliness in relation to Christ himself. This helps frame godliness not as vague moral improvement, but as life rooted in and shaped by the revealed Christ.

sections.heading: Becoming more like you
sections.text:
Lord, how good it would be to reflect you as much as a creature can reflect the Creator. I know I will never be God, and I do not want to pretend otherwise. But I do want more of your likeness—more purity, more love, more steadiness, more obedience.

Stretch my heart so there is more room for holiness. Pull my life more fully toward you, so I live less for myself and more for your honour.
theological_themes: Creaturely likeness to God without collapsing Creator and creature
Growth in holiness
Living for God’s glory rather than self

scripture_references.connection: Peter calls believers to holiness because God is holy. This supports the prayer’s desire to be like God in the way Scripture commands: not by becoming divine, but by sharing in a holy pattern of life.
Paul describes believers being transformed into the image of the Lord. This grounds the request for increasing likeness to God as an ongoing work of grace.

sections.heading: Not settling for spiritual experiences
sections.text:
When you give me sweet moments of prayer, peace, or closeness with you, do not let me turn those gifts into something I admire in myself. And when I feel settled after meeting with you, remind me that I still know so little, love so little, and obey so imperfectly.

Keep me grateful, but keep me hungry. Let every taste of your goodness make me want more of you, not make me satisfied with myself.
theological_themes: Spiritual experiences as gifts, not grounds for self-satisfaction
Humility after communion with God
Pressing on in faith and obedience

scripture_references.connection: Paul refuses to treat his spiritual progress as though he has already arrived, and instead presses on toward Christ. This supports the prayer’s refusal to settle for past experiences or present comfort.

Paul reminds believers that everything they have is received, not self-produced. This speaks to the danger of becoming pleased with one’s spiritual experiences as though they were personal achievements.

sections.heading: Coming close when my heart feels weak
sections.text:
Draw me nearer to you. Teach me to love you, to long for you, to ask boldly, to keep coming back, and not to give up when prayer feels like wrestling.

I need deliverance from the sin that still clings to me. My heart wanders. My affections grow dull. It grieves me that I can lose sight of you, my beloved Lord, even after knowing your kindness. Bring me back again and again.
theological_themes: Persevering prayer
The ongoing struggle with indwelling sin
Spiritual dullness and wandering
Grief over losing sight of Christ

scripture_references.connection: Jesus teaches his disciples to pray always and not lose heart. This supports the prayer’s language of pleading, wrestling, and continuing to seek God when the soul feels weak.

Paul gives voice to the believer’s painful awareness of remaining sin and the cry for deliverance through Jesus Christ. This closely matches the prayer’s longing to be freed from the “body of sin.”},{

sections.heading: Held in love and ready for whatever you give
sections.text:
Wrap my whole life in your love. Keep me wanting you—not only in strong moments, but in ordinary days, tired days, and painful days.

Make me humble. Make me willing to receive your will instead of fighting for my own. Fix my eyes more firmly on you, so I am better prepared to serve when you call me to act, and better prepared to endure when you call me to suffer.
theological_themes: Life held in divine love
Humble surrender to God’s will
Being formed for obedience and suffering
Steadfast focus on God

scripture_references.connection: Paul calls believers to offer themselves to God and be transformed so they may discern his will. This supports the prayer’s desire for humble surrender and a life increasingly directed toward God.

Peter teaches believers who suffer according to God’s will to entrust themselves to the faithful Creator while doing good. This directly supports the prayer’s closing request to be fitted both for doing and for suffering.

Jude calls believers to keep themselves in the love of God while continuing in faith and prayer. This illuminates the prayer’s desire to have the whole life held within divine love and ongoing longing for God.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original phrase about being like God 'as much as it is possible for a creature to be like its Creator' needs careful handling so it is not confused with becoming divine in essence. The adaptation keeps the Creator-creature distinction explicit while preserving the biblical call to holiness and likeness.
significant_interpretive_choices: I rendered 'union with thy will' as the desire for the person’s will to be brought into line with God’s will, rather than as a technical statement about union with Christ.
I interpreted 'mystery of godliness' in connection with Christ-centered godliness rather than general moral seriousness, because the biblical phrase in 1 Timothy 3:16 is explicitly tied to Christ.
I kept the original’s concern about spiritual pride by applying it to pride in prayer, growth, and spiritual experiences, since that is the force of the surrounding lines.
I translated 'doing and suffering' as active obedience and faithful endurance, preserving the Puritan pairing without implying that suffering is to be sought for its own sake.
